base_properties.human_readable: Magisterial-Integralist Reading: AI Governance Bound to Catholic Social Doctrine and Imago Dei Anthropology

stakeholders.name: magisterium_and_curial_offices
stakeholders.situation: Issues encyclicals, dicastery statements, and doctrinal guidance (e.g. Rome Call for AI Ethics) declaring which AI applications are compatible with human dignity as the Church defines it. Convenes signatory institutions, trains bishops and Catholic universities to evaluate technology, and withholds moral legitimacy from noncompliant projects. Bears no direct financial cost of the constraint and gains renewed relevance as an authoritative voice in a domain it did not build.

stakeholders.name: catholic_institutional_hierarchy
stakeholders.situation: Catholic universities, hospital networks, and charitable organizations gain a seat at AI ethics tables, funding for 'human-centered AI' initiatives, and enhanced institutional standing by aligning with Magisterial teaching. They administer local compliance (ethics review boards citing Catholic anthropology) and benefit from the moral capital the doctrine confers.

stakeholders.name: vulnerable_populations
stakeholders.situation: The poor, disabled, elderly, and displaced persons are named as those the doctrine exists to protect from algorithmic exclusion, surveillance, and dehumanizing automation. They rarely participate in drafting the doctrine or the AI systems it governs; the benefit is a protective posture asserted on their behalf, not a power they wield directly.

stakeholders.name: industrial_and_gig_workers
stakeholders.situation: Workers facing algorithmic management and automation are invoked as beneficiaries of Catholic Social Doctrine's labor teachings (dignity of work, subsidiarity, just wage). They stand to gain from Church-backed advocacy against exploitative automation but have no direct enforcement mechanism of their own; their protection depends on the Church's moral suasion succeeding against employers and states.

stakeholders.name: families_and_children
stakeholders.situation: Framed as needing protection from AI systems that would commodify reproduction, surveil children, or substitute for human relational formation. Their interests are asserted by the doctrine but mediated entirely through institutional and parental proxies; they have no independent voice in the governance conversation.

stakeholders.name: technocratic_ai_developers
stakeholders.situation: Firms and labs building AI systems face reputational and, in Catholic-majority jurisdictions, potential regulatory pressure to conform designs to a specific theological anthropology (relational, embodied, finite-yet-transcendent personhood) they did not choose and may not hold. Compliance costs include redesigning systems to avoid classified harms (e.g. certain forms of algorithmic profiling, autonomous lethal decision-making, simulated companionship marketed as substituting for human relationship). Exit means operating outside Catholic-influenced jurisdictions or absorbing reputational costs of public Magisterial censure.

stakeholders.name: transhumanist_researchers
stakeholders.situation: Researchers pursuing cognitive enhancement, life-extension, or mind-uploading research are the doctrine's clearest targets: their entire project is framed as a rejection of proper human finitude and thus incompatible with imago Dei anthropology. They bear reputational marginalization, exclusion from Catholic-affiliated funding and institutions, and public moral condemnation, with no path to accommodation short of abandoning the project's premises.

stakeholders.name: secular_bioethicists
stakeholders.situation: Bioethicists working from secular or pluralist frameworks find their frameworks positioned as deficient or spiritually blind by the doctrine's claim to superior metaphysical grounding. They retain professional mobility and platforms outside Catholic institutions, so the cost is largely one of contested legitimacy in mixed forums rather than material harm.

stakeholders.name: non_catholic_religious_minorities
stakeholders.situation: In jurisdictions where Catholic institutions hold outsized influence over technology policy or education, non-Catholic religious communities may find their own dignity frameworks (e.g. Islamic, Jewish, indigenous, Buddhist accounts of personhood) treated as subordinate or absent from the governing anthropology, despite offering independently coherent grounds for AI restraint.

stakeholders.name: ai_governance_bodies_and_states
stakeholders.situation: National regulators and multilateral bodies (EU AI Act drafters, UNESCO AI ethics panels) receive Magisterial input as one voice among many, weighing it against secular human-rights frameworks, industry lobbying, and pluralist consultation processes. They can adopt, ignore, or selectively cite Catholic Social Doctrine language without being bound by it outside Catholic-influenced jurisdictions.

six_questions.coordination_function: Provides a unified, historically continuous ethical vocabulary (dignity, subsidiarity, common good, solidarity) that Catholic institutions, and some secular actors seeking moral grounding, can use to evaluate and resist AI applications perceived as dehumanizing — filling a real gap where purely procedural or market-based governance frameworks offer no substantive anthropology to adjudicate hard cases (lethal autonomous weapons, simulated companionship, predictive policing).
six_questions.transfer_function: Moves moral authority and institutional legitimacy toward the Magisterium and Catholic-affiliated universities, hospitals, and NGOs (who gain funding, convening power, and policy access), and moves reputational and compliance costs onto AI developers and researchers whose projects conflict with Catholic anthropology — particularly transhumanist and certain surveillance/autonomous-weapons programs. No direct monetary transfer occurs; the currency is legitimacy, access, and moral standing.
six_questions.absent_voices: Non-Catholic theological traditions with independently developed personhood doctrines are largely absent from the drafting process, despite the doctrine claiming to speak for human dignity universally. Transhumanist researchers and technocratic developers are named as targets but are not invited co-authors of the anthropology that constrains them. Vulnerable populations, workers, and families — the named beneficiaries — are represented by advocacy rather than direct participation.
six_questions.disappearance_rationale: From the Magisterium's own account, disappearance would leave AI governance to secular and market logics it regards as insufficiently protective of the person, producing real harm to vulnerable groups (world_rearranges). From a technocratic developer's account, disappearance would simply remove one non-binding moral voice among many competing frameworks that already coexist in a pluralist governance landscape, changing little in actual regulatory outcomes (world_unchanged). The verdict depends on how much causal weight one assigns to moral suasion absent binding legal force.

commentary.narrative_context: This story instantiates the magisterial-integralist reading of the human_dignity_ai_governance kernel: human dignity as an ontological gift (imago Dei), infinite and inalienable, discernible through faith and reason together, with the Magisterium possessing unique interpretive authority to guide AI governance toward the common good. This reading is one of four sibling readings of the same kernel (secular_humanist, techno_optimist, pluralist_pragmatic); it is authored here as a self-contained, ε-invariant constraint on its own terms, not as a synthesis or comparison. The Church's actual instruments (Rome Call for AI Ethics, papal statements, dicastery documents, Catholic university ethics boards) rely on moral suasion and institutional gatekeeping rather than binding law, which keeps extractiveness moderate rather than high.
key_agents: magisterium_and_curial_offices: primary agenda-setter, institutional/analytical exit, sets doctrinal terms
catholic_institutional_hierarchy: secondary beneficiary/administrator, gains funding and standing
vulnerable_populations, industrial_and_gig_workers, families_and_children: named beneficiaries, powerless-to-moderate, represented rather than participating
technocratic_ai_developers, transhumanist_researchers: primary targets, bear reputational and compliance costs
secular_bioethicists, non_catholic_religious_minorities: secondary payers, contested legitimacy costs
ai_governance_bodies_and_states: analytical observers, weigh Magisterial input against competing frameworks
commentary.logic_rationale: Extractiveness is authored at 0.42 (moderate) because the doctrine demands substantial structural change to AI design and deployment but has no binding legal force outside Catholic-affiliated institutions — compliance is voluntary, and the cost imposed on developers is reputational/legitimacy-based rather than coercive. Suppression is authored lower (0.28) for the same reason: alternatives are not closed off by law, only by moral pressure and institutional gatekeeping (exclusion from Catholic-affiliated funding, public censure). Theater ratio (0.3) reflects that a meaningful share of activity is genuine doctrinal development and institutional coordination (Catholic universities running real ethics review), but a growing share over the interval is symbolic signing of non-binding declarations (Rome Call signatories) that generate reputational capital without altering practice. Resistance is authored relatively high (0.6) because technocratic and transhumanist actors actively contest the doctrine's claim to unique interpretive authority over a domain they consider properly secular or technical.
commentary.directionality_logic: Beneficiaries (vulnerable populations, workers, families) receive low d — protective advocacy asserted on their behalf without their direct participation, consistent with the beneficiary end. Technocratic developers and transhumanist researchers receive high d — they are the doctrine's explicit targets, bearing reputational, funding-access, and institutional-legitimacy costs channeled through the same anthropological framework that protects the beneficiaries. The Magisterium and Catholic institutional hierarchy sit at the agenda-setting end: they administer the doctrine, gain institutional relevance and moral capital, and bear none of the compliance costs they impose on others. Secular bioethicists and non-Catholic religious minorities are payers of contested legitimacy rather than material cost — their mobility (secular bioethicists) or structural marginalization (religious minorities in Catholic-influenced jurisdictions) differentiates their positions despite superficially similar 'payer' framing.
commentary.mandatrophy_analysis: The founding problem — the absence of any substantive anthropology in purely procedural or market-driven AI governance — remains genuinely live wherever lethal autonomous weapons, algorithmic surveillance, and simulated companionship products raise questions no secular procedural framework fully resolves. This is not a dead mandate riding on inertia: the coordination function (a coherent, historically continuous vocabulary for resisting dehumanizing technology) is real and actively invoked by both Catholic and non-Catholic actors in international forums. The tangled-rope classification, rather than pure snare, follows from this genuine coordination function coexisting with asymmetric extraction: the same anthropological claims that protect vulnerable populations also assert exclusive interpretive authority over a domain the Church does not uniquely occupy, and channel legitimacy and institutional advantage toward Catholic actors specifically rather than toward the protected populations themselves.
commentary.kernel_context: This constraint instantiates the magisterial_integralist_reading of the human_dignity_ai_governance kernel. The kernel here is the standing question of what grounds human dignity for purposes of AI governance and who has authority to adjudicate it. This reading holds: dignity is an ontological gift from God (imago Dei), infinite and inalienable, knowable through faith AND reason jointly, with the Magisterium possessing unique teaching authority to interpret Catholic Social Doctrine's application to technology. Sibling readings instantiate structurally different constraints from the same contested kernel: the secular_humanist_reading grounds dignity in rational autonomy and UDHR-style universal rights, adjudicated through democratic deliberation rather than religious authority; the techno_optimist_reading treats dignity as enhanced rather than threatened by AI, minimizing governance restriction; the pluralist_pragmatic_reading treats dignity itself as contested and seeks negotiated, metaphysically-neutral frameworks. Each sibling reading has (or would have) its own ε, its own beneficiary/victim structure, and its own classification — this story does not average or hedge across them.

omegas.question: Does the Magisterium possess a legitimate unique claim to interpretive authority over AI governance's anthropological foundations, or is this claim itself an extractive move by one institutional tradition among many competing traditions?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Track whether Magisterial AI ethics guidance is adopted, cited, or substantively incorporated by non-Catholic governance bodies (EU, UN, national regulators) versus merely acknowledged as one input among many equally-weighted inputs; sustained substantive adoption over decoration would support the coordination reading, mere acknowledgment would support the extraction reading.
omegas.impact: If the Magisterium's authority claim is vindicated by substantive uptake, this reading functions closer to genuine rope (real coordination benefit, low extraction). If the claim is resisted or merely tokenized, the tangled_rope classification undersells the extractive component and the reading functions closer to a legitimacy-capture snare targeting technocratic and transhumanist actors while the claimed universal benefit to vulnerable populations remains largely rhetorical.
omegas.description: Whether unique Magisterial authority over AI ethics is genuine coordination or institutional legitimacy capture.

omegas.question: Will the doctrine's reliance on moral suasion and voluntary adoption remain stable, or will Catholic-influenced jurisdictions move toward binding legal incorporation of Catholic Social Doctrine anthropology into AI regulation (e.g. in countries with strong Catholic constitutional influence)?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Monitor legislative activity in Catholic-majority jurisdictions (Poland, Philippines, parts of Latin America) for direct statutory incorporation of imago Dei-derived anthropological restrictions on AI design, as distinct from non-binding ethical guidance.
omegas.impact: A shift from voluntary to binding enforcement would sharply raise both extractiveness and suppression, potentially moving this reading's classification from tangled_rope toward snare as the enforcement mechanism becomes coercive rather than persuasive.
omegas.description: Whether enforcement will remain voluntary/persuasive or harden into binding legal coercion.

omegas.question: Is 'the Church has unique authority' a claim internal to this reading's own coherence, or does authoring it as a standalone constraint (rather than folding it into a broader 'religious traditions vs secular governance' axis) understate how much this reading's classification depends on where the kernel boundary is drawn?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Compare this reading's cs_structure and classification against a hypothetical alternative decomposition that treats 'religious authority over technology governance' as the kernel (with Catholic, Islamic, and other traditions as sibling readings within it) rather than 'human dignity grounding' as the kernel with this reading as one of four dignity-grounding accounts.
omegas.impact: Under the authored framing (dignity-grounding as kernel), this reading's distinguishing axiom is theological anthropology; under the alternative framing (religious-authority-over-tech as kernel), the distinguishing axiom would instead be Magisterial exclusivity versus other traditions' authority claims, which could shift the axiom set and reading_relations substantially, particularly with respect to non_catholic_religious_minorities.
omegas.description: Alternative kernel-boundary framing (dignity-grounding vs. religious-authority) would change the axiom set and possibly the reading relations.

network.dual_formulation_note: This story is one of four sibling readings of the human_dignity_ai_governance kernel. Each reading (magisterial_integralist, secular_humanist, techno_optimist, pluralist_pragmatic) grounds dignity differently and therefore authors a different beneficiary/victim structure, a different ε, and a different classification for what is nominally 'the same' AI governance debate. The magisterial_integralist_reading has moderate extractiveness (0.42) driven by voluntary-but-substantial demands on AI design; the secular_humanist_reading would author extraction driven by democratic-legitimacy claims rather than theological ones; the techno_optimist_reading would author near-zero coordination-side extraction and instead treat restriction itself as the cost; the pluralist_pragmatic_reading would author lower extraction overall by design, since it explicitly avoids privileging any single metaphysical foundation. These are not four measurements of one constraint — they are four distinct constraints sharing a contested kernel, linked here for contamination and coupling analysis.
